speaker: Eric Jang
title: What rebuilding AlphaGo teaches us about self-play, RL, and future of LLMs - Eric Jang
question: In large-scale AI training, why do individually promising algorithmic speedups often fail to stack when combined?
guest: The research taste for executing well on the bitter lesson is knowing how much it can buy you and how much is too much to ask at any given moment. In the fullness of time, compute is the single most important determinant of how things work, and as you scale up energy, compute, and parameters, intelligence falls out and no algorithmic detail really matters beyond that. In the present day, however, we do not have infinite compute, parameters, or arbitrarily good initialization, so we come up with heuristics that approximate those advantages. Those heuristics are often somewhat redundant, which is why many compute multipliers do not stack—they capture correlated benefits. Three years down the line, when GPUs have gotten even stronger, they stack even less well. At any given point in time, the benefit of any compute multiplier is transitory. With modern Blackwell and Ada GPUs compared to older V100s, many algorithmic tricks that sped up convergence in earlier systems simply stop mattering as much.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the speedups are not independent: they tend to draw on the same limited pool of inefficiency, and each was measured against a baseline that the others change.

Many tricks are different routes to the same underlying gain. Better optimizers, learning-rate schedules, normalization, initialization and architecture tweaks often all improve conditioning or reduce gradient noise, so once one has captured that slack, the next finds little left. Reported gains are also frequently inflated by weak, under-tuned baselines; a well-tuned baseline already absorbs much of the benefit.

Interactions matter too. Each method shifts the optimal hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, warmup, regularization), so combining them without jointly re-tuning can cancel gains or destabilize training, and joint tuning is prohibitively expensive at scale. Some methods rely on conflicting assumptions, such as pairing aggressive data pruning with a technique that needs diverse data.

Finally, many gains fail to transfer. Speedups found on small models, short runs or particular datasets often shrink at larger scale or longer horizons, and per-step improvements may not survive wall-clock overheads or Amdahl-style bottlenecks in the hardware and data pipeline. Benchmarks like MLCommons AlgoPerf were created largely to expose this.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Individually promising algorithmic speedups rarely stack cleanly because they compete for shared optimization slack, destabilize coupled training dynamics, and clash with hardware constraints. Many techniques—whether architectural tweaks, data curricula, or novel optimizers—target the same underlying inefficiencies, such as ill-conditioned curvature or weak regularization. Once one method captures that gain, or once a baseline schedule is properly tuned, adding others yields diminishing returns or degrades convergence through over-regularization.

Furthermore, methods validated in isolation at small scale often interact destructively at frontier scale, where training operates near the edge of stability. Combining interventions alters effective learning rates, gradient variance, and critical batch sizes, triggering loss spikes or divergence unless hyperparameters are jointly retuned at prohibitive compute cost. Finally, systems bottlenecks enforce Amdahl’s law: algorithms that reduce theoretical FLOPs or step counts frequently introduce irregular memory access, extra kernel launches, or distributed synchronization overhead, shifting bottlenecks from compute to memory bandwidth or interconnect communication and erasing wall-clock gains.

noweb.answer:
Individually promising algorithmic speedups rarely stack in large-scale AI training because they frequently target overlapping bottlenecks, destabilize coupled dynamics, and collide with systems constraints. Many interventions—whether second-order optimizers, normalization tweaks, or data curricula—implicitly exploit the same underlying slack in a baseline, such as poor curvature conditioning or a suboptimal effective learning rate; once one method resolves that inefficiency, little headroom remains for another.

Furthermore, techniques are usually validated in isolation, yet training hyperparameters are tightly coupled. Combining sharper updates, architectural changes, and aggressive schedules narrows the optimization stability margin at scale, triggering loss spikes or divergence that force practitioners to lower learning rates and erase the expected gains. Many apparent speedups also merely front-load early transient progress on short validation runs without improving asymptotic scaling, causing their benefits to vanish over full compute horizons and well-tuned learning rate decay schedules. Finally, methods that save training steps often introduce extra memory traffic, distributed communication, or unfused operations that reduce hardware utilization, turning theoretical sample-efficiency gains into negligible wall-clock speedups under Amdahl’s law.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Speedups often fail to stack because they aren't independent. Many of them fix the same underlying inefficiency. A better optimizer, a tuned learning-rate schedule, improved normalization and smarter initialization can all be ways of handling poor conditioning or unstable early training. Once one of them has captured that slack, the others have little left to improve, so the combined gain is closer to the largest single gain than to the product of all of them.

Baselines and tuning are a second problem. A trick is usually tested against a weak or lightly tuned baseline. Part of its reported gain is really just compensation for bad hyperparameters, which disappears once the baseline is strong. Tricks also change the best learning rate, batch size or warmup, so tricks tuned one at a time can conflict when combined.

Scale matters too. Gains measured on small models or short runs often shrink, or even reverse, at frontier scale. Many tricks speed up early convergence without changing where the run ends up.

Finally, there's an Amdahl's-law effect on the systems side. Cutting FLOPs in one component moves the bottleneck to memory bandwidth, communication or data loading, so wall-clock speedups compound much less than the headline numbers suggest.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Individually promising algorithmic speedups rarely stack because they often address the same underlying optimization bottlenecks. Techniques like improved optimizers, normalization schemes, warmups, and better initializations frequently accelerate training by stabilizing activations, reducing gradient noise, or improving loss-landscape conditioning; once one method fixes that pathology, another targeting it yields diminishing returns rather than multiplicative gains.

Even when methods target distinct aspects of training, they interact nonlinearly and can interfere destructively. Combining aggressive preconditioning, learning-rate schedules, low-precision arithmetic, or data-efficiency tricks often introduces numerical instability or shifts the optimal hyperparameter regime, forcing expensive joint retuning that erases much of the theoretical speedup.

Finally, large-scale training is constrained by shifting system and statistical bottlenecks. Accelerating convergence or reducing FLOPs per step quickly exposes fixed overheads such as inter-node communication, memory bandwidth, and pipeline bubbles. Because well-tuned frontier baselines already operate close to hardware and data-efficiency limits, gains that look dramatic in isolation tend to compress sharply when layered together.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Speedups measured in isolation are usually relative to the same baseline, so multiplying them assumes each still saves as much once the others are in place. Two techniques may eliminate the same memory transfers. And once one technique makes GPU computation faster, communication between GPUs can take up a larger share of each step, leaving less room for another compute optimization to help.

Training speed also depends on how many steps it takes to reach a target quality. Changes to batch size, numerical precision, or the optimizer can interact, so settings that worked well individually may need to be retuned when combined. A faster step can lose its advantage if the model needs more steps. The meaningful test is the combined system’s wall-clock time to reach the same quality at the intended training scale.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A speedup measured on its own is measured against the original training run. Once one change is in place, the next change acts on a different baseline. For example, if two techniques both eliminate some of the same computation, that work can only be saved once. And if faster computation leaves GPUs waiting for communication, further compute savings may barely change the time per step.

The techniques can also interact through training dynamics. An optimizer and a batch-size change might each reduce the time to reach a target accuracy on their own, yet together require a different learning rate or more training steps. What matters is how much wall-clock time the combination saves at the same model quality. Multiplying the standalone speedups assumes each technique retains its full relative benefit after the others are applied.
